name: Apache NiFi
summary: A Java dataflow server you program by drawing a graph of processors in a web UI, with buffered queues, back pressure and a record of where every piece of data went.
intro: NiFi runs in a JVM and serves its web UI and REST API from the same process. You build a flow on a canvas: processors (hundreds ship with it, such as `ConsumeKafka`, `CaptureChangeMySQL`, `PutS3Object` and `PutDatabaseRecord`) joined by connections. Each piece of data moving through is a FlowFile: a map of string attributes plus a content stream of zero or more bytes. Every connection is a queue with limits, by default 10,000 FlowFiles or 1 GB, and when a queue hits its limit the upstream processor stops being scheduled. That is back pressure. A flow controller hands threads to processors. Three disk repositories hold the state: a write-ahead log of the FlowFiles currently in the flow, a content repository with the bytes, and a provenance repository that indexes every event (created, modified, routed, sent) so you can trace an object’s lineage, view its content at any step and replay it. Provenance is kept for 30 days or 10 GB by default.

Changes on the canvas take effect immediately, without a deploy step. In a cluster every node runs the same flow on a different share of the data, with a coordinator elected through ZooKeeper or, since NiFi 2, Kubernetes. MiNiFi is a small agent, in Java or as a native C++ binary, that runs a subset of processors next to sensors and servers and forwards data to NiFi. Flows are versioned through Flow Registry Clients. Since NiFi 2 these can store flows directly in GitHub or GitLab, and the separate NiFi Registry service is deprecated. NiFi 2.0 (November 2024) requires Java 21, added a Python processor API (still labelled beta) and removed many old components.
strengths: Visual, live editing: you can see queues fill up and change a running flow one component at a time
Built-in provenance records the lineage of every FlowFile, which helps with audits, debugging and replaying data
Bounded queues with back pressure and prioritisation let slow destinations push back instead of losing data
A large library of processors for files, SFTP, HTTP, Kafka, databases, cloud storage and queues, extensible in Java or Python
Runs anywhere from a single Docker container to a cluster, with MiNiFi agents at the edge
limits: Flows live in a canvas, not code: reviewing and testing changes is harder than with SQL or Python pipelines, and large flows become hard to follow
Running a cluster is real work: JVM heap tuning, several disk repositories, ZooKeeper or Kubernetes coordination, TLS and user management
It routes and reshapes data in flight; modelling inside the warehouse (SQL models and their tests) is a job for tools like dbt
Upgrades break things: NiFi 1.x lost support in December 2024, 2.0 removed many processors (HBase, Kudu, Kafka 2.6 and others), and NiFi Registry is now deprecated with removal planned for 3.0
Python processors are still marked beta and not recommended for production

items.name: NiFi
items.text: The JVM process with the canvas, REST API, flow controller and the FlowFile, content and provenance repositories. Runs alone or as a cluster.

items.name: NiFi Stateless
items.text: A separate download for running a flow in stateless mode. Since 2.0, process groups inside a normal NiFi can also use a stateless execution mode.

items.name: MiNiFi
items.text: A small agent in Java, or a native C++ build for Linux and Windows with a subset of processors, that collects data at the source and forwards it to NiFi with provenance intact.

items.name: Git-based Flow Registry Clients
items.text: Store versioned flows directly in GitHub or GitLab repositories, with branches since 2.10.

items.name: NiFi Registry
items.text: The separate flow-versioning service. Deprecated by community vote in February 2026 and planned for removal in NiFi 3.0.

items.name: NiFi Toolkit
items.text: Command-line tools, including the NiFi CLI for managing nodes, flows and registry clients.

story: Intelligence agencies move huge volumes of data between networks that use different formats and protocols, under strict rules about who may see what. In late 2006 a team at the US National Security Agency, led by Joe Witt, started building a tool for this, called Niagarafiles. It was based on flow-based programming: small black-box processors joined by bounded queues, managed live through a visual interface, with a record of where every piece of data came from.

In November 2014 the NSA released it through its Technology Transfer Program, its first in a series of open-source releases, and it entered the Apache Incubator as NiFi. It became a top-level Apache project in July 2015. Hortonworks agreed in August 2015 to buy Onyara, whose engineers had been the key contributors to the government project, and built Hortonworks DataFlow on NiFi. Cloudera took that business over when it merged with Hortonworks in 2019.

NiFi made dataflow something you could watch and change while it ran. A decade on, its foundations had aged: NiFi 1 was stuck on Jetty 9.4, Spring 5.3 and AngularJS 1.8, so NiFi 2.0 (2024) moved to Java 21, rebuilt the UI and dropped many old components.

choices.why: Processors that only talk through queues are naturally concurrent and asynchronous, and capping the queues gives back pressure, so a slow system pushes back instead of losing data.

choices.choice: Change the flow while it runs
choices.why: Production environments often can’t be reproduced in a lab, so NiFi treats a flow like clay: each change applies immediately to one component without stopping the rest.
Compliance and security rules demand knowing where data came from and where it went, so lineage and content history are part of the core, not an add-on.
Processors can route on a FlowFile’s attributes without reading its content, while the bytes stay in the content repository, which uses copy-on-write.
